claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC HEA nanoscale multilayers under sustained loading is governed by the interaction of dislocation activity and interfacial sliding.
The balance between dislocation activity and interfacial sliding is controlled by lattice mismatch at FCC/BCC interfaces.
The balance between dislocation activity and interfacial sliding is controlled by short-range order at FCC/BCC interfaces.
The proposed system is an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy nanoscale multilayer coating.
Sustained uniaxial loading at elevated temperature is proposed to induce creep deformation.
The proposed loading stress is below the yield strength of the individual layers.
Lattice mismatch at FCC/BCC interfaces creates barriers to dislocation motion.
Short-range order at FCC/BCC interfaces creates barriers to dislocation motion.
Barriers to dislocation motion promote interfacial sliding as a competing deformation mechanism.
The degree of lattice mismatch influences the interfacial stress distribution and energy barriers for dislocation nucleation and motion.
The extent of short-range order influences the interfacial stress distribution and energy barriers for dislocation nucleation and motion.
Multilayers with higher lattice mismatch and more pronounced short-range order will exhibit reduced dislocation activity relative to multilayers with lower mismatch and less short-range order.
Multilayers with higher lattice mismatch and more pronounced short-range order will exhibit increased interfacial sliding relative to multilayers with lower mismatch and less short-range order.
Multilayers with higher lattice mismatch and more pronounced short-range order will have a lower creep rate than multilayers with lower mismatch and less short-range order.
The proposed mechanism applies when atomic diffusion is active but melting does not occur.
